title: Interest Rates: Types of Rates, Continuous Compounding, and Zero Curve Bootstrapping
prerequisites: Basic understanding of time value of money and present value discounting
Familiarity with exponential functions and natural logarithms
Concept of bond coupons and par value
learningOutcomes: Distinguish Treasury, LIBOR, Repo, and OIS benchmark interest rates and explain their credit risk profiles.
Convert between discrete compounding frequencies and continuous compounding using the exact formula R_c = m * ln(1 + R_m / m).
Price coupon-bearing bonds by treating them as portfolios of zero-coupon cash flows discounted at dedicated zero rates.
Execute the recursive bootstrap method to extract zero rates sequentially from market bond yields.
Explain why the 2008 crisis forced derivatives discounting from LIBOR to OIS.

sections.title: Benchmark Rates & The Risk-Free Hierarchy
sections.pedagogicalObjective: Understand Treasury, LIBOR, Repo, and OIS rates and why Treasury yields are artificially depressed.
keyPoints: Treasury bills have regulatory and tax advantages that depress yields below pure risk-free levels.
Repo rates represent secured collateralized borrowing.
OIS represents the true modern risk-free benchmark for collateralized derivatives.

sections.title: Continuous vs Discrete Compounding
sections.pedagogicalObjective: Master the mathematical limit as compounding frequency reaches infinity and apply equivalence conversions.
keyPoints: Compounding frequency increases terminal wealth up to the theoretical limit e^(rT).
Conversion formula: R_c = m * ln(1 + R_m / m).
A 10% semiannual rate equals 9.758% continuously compounded.

sections.title: Zero Rates and Bond Pricing Reality
sections.pedagogicalObjective: Demonstrate why discounting coupons at a single YTM is flawed and value bonds using zero rates.
keyPoints: Zero rates represent pure single-payment loans with zero reinvestment risk.
Bond price is the exact sum of discounted cash flows: P = sum(C_i * e^(-r_i * t_i)) + M * e^(-r_n * t_n).
Par yield is the coupon rate setting bond price equal to face value 100.
sections.formulaUsed: P = sum(C_i * e^(-r_i * t_i)) + M * e^(-r_n * t_n)

sections.title: The Bootstrap Method for Zero Curve Construction
sections.pedagogicalObjective: Sequentially unlock the continuous zero curve from cash rates and par coupon bonds.
keyPoints: Short-term bills directly provide spot zero rates.
Longer bonds discount earlier cash flows at known zero rates to isolate the final zero rate.
The bootstrap builds the entire term structure without complex matrix inversion.

sections.title: The 2008 Crisis and the OIS Revolution
sections.pedagogicalObjective: Analyze why the derivatives industry abandoned LIBOR discounting for OIS post-2008.
keyPoints: Pre-2008, LIBOR was used as the universal risk-free rate.
The Lehman collapse blew out the LIBOR-OIS spread to 364 bps, revealing bank credit risk.
Daily collateral cash earns the overnight rate, mandating OIS discounting.

misconceptions.misconception: Treasury bond yields represent the purest risk-free interest rates for derivatives pricing.
misconceptions.authorRebuttal: Treasury rates are artificially depressed by regulatory capital requirements and tax perks. OIS represents true risk-free institutional funding.

misconceptions.misconception: A 10% semiannual interest rate is equivalent to a 10% continuous interest rate.
misconceptions.authorRebuttal: Intra-year compounding makes 10% semiannual equal 9.758% continuously compounded: R_c = 2 * ln(1.05) = 9.758%.

misconceptions.misconception: A bond's Yield to Maturity represents the guaranteed realized return for the holder.
misconceptions.authorRebuttal: YTM only equals realized return if every single coupon is reinvested at that exact same YTM, which is impossible across real dynamic yield curves.

activeRecallQuiz.scenario: Given a 1-year Treasury bond paying a 6% semiannual coupon trading at par 100, and a known 6-month zero rate of 5% (continuously compounded), what is the 1-year continuous zero rate?
activeRecallQuiz.question: What is the 1-year continuously compounded zero rate extracted via the bootstrap method?
activeRecallQuiz.explanation: The 6-month coupon of $3 discounts at 5% to 3 * e^(-0.05 * 0.5) = $2.9259. The remaining $97.0741 is paid at 1 year ($103). Solving 103 * e^(-r_1 * 1.0) = 97.0741 gives r_1 = -ln(97.0741 / 103) = 5.93%.

coreTakeaways: Treasury yields carry regulatory distortions; OIS represents true risk-free institutional discounting.
Continuous compounding A = P * e^(rT) is the mathematical bedrock of all modern derivatives pricing.
A coupon bond is a portfolio of zero-coupon payouts, each requiring its own maturity-matched zero rate.
The bootstrap method sequentially extracts continuous zero rates from market instruments without matrix inversion.
Post-2008 derivatives valuation strictly mandates OIS discounting to reflect collateral earning the overnight rate.
